title: I am the gate (John 10:1–10)
hook: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man questioned three times, thrown out, and found again. Your line was one thing I know. What one thing did you say you know? Day six hundred nineteen.

A sheepfold on a hillside: a rough circle of stone walls, chest high, with one gap for an opening. At night the sheep are led inside, safe from wolves and thieves. Jesus is still talking to the same listeners as yesterday, the ones who threw the healed man out, and he tells them a picture-story about sheep, a gatekeeper, thieves who climb over the wall, and a shepherd who walks in through the door. John says plainly that they didn't understand it. So Jesus tries again, more directly.

First, the shepherd. The sheep hear his voice, and "he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Notice how personal that is. Not a herd. Names. Then the surprise: "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture." The King James says door. Some modern Bibles say gate. Either way, it's the opening in the wall. John has given us I am sayings before: bread, light. Now, the way in. People often tell how a shepherd in that region, at night, might lie down across the gap in the wall and sleep there, so that nothing could get in or out without stepping over him. Whether or not every shepherd did that, it's a good picture of what Jesus is saying. Look at the words: go in and out. A gate isn't only for locking in. It's for safety at night and freedom in the morning. In, to rest. Out, to pasture. Then the verse behind today's line: "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly." The Greek word behind abundantly means more than enough, overflowing, beyond what's needed. Not just surviving. Not just getting by. Life with something left over. Christians often hold this line as a picture of what faith is meant to be: not a smaller life fenced in by rules, but a bigger one, with a safe place to come home to.

Here's the practice: choose one abundant thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of your day as it's going to go. How much of it is just getting by? Errands, emails, getting through. That's real, and it's fine. Now picture one small thing you could add that is more than necessary. A longer walk. A real conversation. Cooking something properly. Ten minutes outside. Music you love, played loud. Choose one. If you pray, you can give thanks for the life you have, and ask for it in full. If you don't, just savor the thought of the thing you chose. The bell holds the time.
Sheepfold. The walled hillside pen Jesus pictures, with one gap for a gate: the shepherd leads his sheep in to rest, and out to pasture.
Your line: life to the full. Today, do the one abundant thing you chose, and do it without hurrying. Day six hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Christians often quote John 10:10 when describing the life they hope faith brings.

notes: Index title says 'gate'; KJV says 'door'. The script explains both.

The shepherd sleeping across the sheepfold's opening is a commonly told picture (from travelers' accounts of Middle Eastern shepherds); presented as 'people often tell' and 'whether or not every shepherd did'. Confirm.
Order of I am sayings: this script calls 'the door' the third (after bread 6:35 and light 8:12). Confirm consistency with day 620 (good shepherd as fourth).
John 10:6 says they did not understand; confirm.
